scenes.tts: Chapter one ended with a pull running through every link of the chain. Can that pull change a link itself? To find out, start where the pull begins, inside the cell.
scenes.narration: Chapter one ended with a pull running through every link of the chain. Can that pull change a link itself? To find out, start where the pull begins, inside the cell.
scenes.caption: Chapter one ended with a pull running through every link of the chain. Can that pull change a link itself? To find out, start where the pull begins, inside the cell.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD from chapter 1, same colours, same place: the side-on epithelium, a row of four tall GREY cells with nuclei on the thin ORANGE basement membrane sheet, the wavy ORANGE matrix ropes below, YELLOW calcium dots drifting in the fluid above. Every chain from chapter 1 glows faintly in its colours (BLUE cadherin chains between cells, PURPLE integrin chains at the base, PINK keratin cables). A GOLD pulse travels slowly through the web, cell to cell and down into the matrix, as at the end of chapter 1. On 'Can that pull change a link itself?' the white question 'Can pull change a link?' fades in at the top and stays. On 'inside the cell', the camera starts moving into the base of the second cell, toward its integrin chain. Colour map unchanged from chapter 1: YELLOW calcium, BLUE cadherin, PURPLE integrin, TEAL adaptors, GREEN actin, PINK keratin, ORANGE matrix, GOLD pull, GREY cells. New in this chapter only: CORAL = myosin II motor.
Title 'Links That Feel the Pull' fades in for 2 s over the moving camera; the question at the top fades out under it. The GOLD pulse keeps travelling.

scenes.tts: Here, a motor protein called myosin two grips the actin cables and slides them past one another. So the cell can keep its own chains under load. That pull reaches every link, down to the matrix.
scenes.narration: Here, a motor protein called myosin II grips the actin cables and slides them past one another. So the cell can keep its own chains under load. That pull reaches every link, down to the matrix.
scenes.caption: Here, a motor protein called myosin II grips the actin cables and slides them past one another. So the cell can keep its own chains under load. That pull reaches every link, down to the matrix.
scenes.visual: Camera settles inside the cell, near its base: two overlapping GREEN actin cables with opposite polarity fill the middle of the frame; small simple arrowheads mark their opposite orientations. The upper cable is anchored at its right end to the integrin chain at the membrane (PURPLE integrin, TEAL talin bar, ORANGE fibronectin below), while the lower cable continues left into the actin network. Show first, then name: a short CORAL bipolar assembly, drawn as a labelled bar with simple motor blobs at both ends, bridges the cables. Its two ends step toward the cables' barbed ends, sliding the antiparallel cables relative to one another in a steady loop. Label 'myosin II' in CORAL appears after the movement starts. On 'under load', small GOLD arrows point away from the motor assembly along the tensed cables, and a GOLD pulse runs from the anchored cable down through TEAL and PURPLE into the ORANGE strand, which straightens. Label 'cell-generated pull'. Schematic shapes only; do not draw myosin's molecular structure.

scenes.tts: Look closer at the integrin chain's adaptor, talin. Its long rod contains thirteen small bundles of alpha helices. Each bundle is folded up tight.
scenes.narration: Look closer at the integrin chain's adaptor, talin. Its long rod contains 13 small bundles of α-helices. Each bundle is folded up tight.
scenes.caption: Look closer at the integrin chain's adaptor, talin. Its long rod contains 13 small bundles of α-helices. Each bundle is folded up tight.
scenes.visual: Zoom on the TEAL talin bar between the PURPLE integrin tail (bottom) and the GREEN actin cable (top), until the bar runs across most of the frame width. Show first, then name: the bar resolves into a row of 13 small TEAL rounded blocks in a line, like beads on a string; the blocks gently jiggle. A small counter in white ticks '1 ... 13' along the row as each block brightens briefly in turn. Label 'talin rod: 13 helix bundles'. Corner label 'schematic'. Labelled blocks only; do not draw the helices or any molecular structure.

scenes.tts: Some of these bundles hide binding sites for vinculin, the second adaptor you met in chapter one. While a bundle stays folded, its site stays tucked away inside.
scenes.narration: Some of these bundles hide binding sites for vinculin, the second adaptor you met in chapter one. While a bundle stays folded, its site stays tucked away inside.
scenes.caption: Some of these bundles hide binding sites for vinculin, the second adaptor you met in chapter one. While a bundle stays folded, its site stays tucked away inside.
scenes.visual: Three representative TEAL blocks turn semi-transparent for a moment, revealing a small bright white dot inside each (label 'hidden vinculin site'), then become opaque again so the dots are hidden. A corner label says 'examples, not a count'. Off to the side, two small free TEAL blocks labelled 'vinculin' drift in the cytoplasm, bumping against the folded blocks and bouncing off. The CORAL myosin motors keep moving on the GREEN cable above at a slow idle; the GOLD arrows are dim.

scenes.tts: Now take a purified piece of the talin rod, outside any cell, and stretch it. A test piece from vinculin waits beside it. What happens to those hidden sites? Make a guess.
scenes.narration: Now take a purified piece of the talin rod, outside any cell, and stretch it. A test piece from vinculin waits beside it. What happens to those hidden sites? Make a guess.
scenes.caption: Now take a purified piece of the talin rod, outside any cell, and stretch it. A test piece from vinculin waits beside it. What happens to those hidden sites? Make a guess.
scenes.visual: The cell fades back; the talin row is now alone in a clean frame (label 'purified talin rod piece'). Its left end is held by a small GREY clamp; on 'stretch it', a GOLD arrow pulls the right end slowly to the right and the whole row tautens. On 'test piece from vinculin', two small TEAL blocks labelled 'vinculin head (test piece)' appear beside it. The question card appears at the top in white: 'Stretch talin: hidden sites?'

Thinking pause. The question card stays. The talin row is held taut by the GOLD arrow, which breathes slightly; the three hidden-site blocks pulse faintly; the free vinculin blocks drift in place. Nothing else changes.

scenes.tts: The bundles unfold, and the hidden sites open. The vinculin test pieces bind to them. Back in a cell, activated vinculin can add another tie to actin. So pulling can recruit reinforcements.
scenes.narration: The bundles unfold, and the hidden sites open. The vinculin test pieces bind to them. Back in a cell, activated vinculin can add another tie to actin. So pulling can recruit reinforcements.
scenes.caption: The bundles unfold, and the hidden sites open. The vinculin test pieces bind to them. Back in a cell, activated vinculin can add another tie to actin. So pulling can recruit reinforcements.
scenes.visual: On 'unfold', the three marked TEAL rounded blocks lengthen into narrow dashed-outline blocks labelled 'unfolded'; the white site dots move from inside to the exposed edge. On 'test pieces bind', the TEAL blocks labelled 'vinculin head (test piece)' dock onto the exposed white dots with a small flash. On 'Back in a cell', the frame dissolves to the cellular chain and each test piece is replaced by a labelled block, 'activated vinculin', beside the stretched talin between PURPLE integrin and GREEN actin. Each activated vinculin sends a short extra tie to the GREEN cable, as a branch beside talin. The GOLD pulse now runs through talin and the new ties, split among them. White label 'pull can recruit reinforcements' appears and stays. Schematic blocks only; no molecular structures.

scenes.tts: Magnetic tweezers pulled a bead tied to a single mouse talin rod. Bundles unfolded at about five to twenty-five piconewtons, trillionths of a newton. They refolded as force fell. A model using those rates suggests the rod can buffer force.
scenes.narration: Magnetic tweezers pulled a bead tied to a single mouse talin rod. Bundles unfolded at about 5 to 25 piconewtons, trillionths of a newton. They refolded as force fell. A model using those rates suggests the rod can buffer force.
scenes.caption: Magnetic tweezers pulled a bead tied to a single mouse talin rod. Bundles unfolded at about 5 to 25 piconewtons, trillionths of a newton. They refolded as force fell. A model using those rates suggests the rod can buffer force.
scenes.visual: Split the frame: left, a small schematic of the method, a GREY bead tethered to one end of one TEAL talin row, the other end fixed to a surface, and a grey magnet above the bead pulling it upward (label 'magnetic tweezers: one molecule'). Right, a horizontal force bar in GOLD from 0 to 30 pN, labelled 'force (pN)', with a shaded band from 5 to 25 pN labelled 'unfolding events (about)'. As the GOLD level rises through the band, representative bundles on the left open at different forces; do not imply 13 independent unfolding events. As force falls, the opened bundles refold without assigning a single refolding threshold. On 'buffer force', a white label 'model: force buffer' appears beside the bar. Loop once more gently. Corner label 'schematic, not data'. No curve is drawn.

scenes.tts: The cadherin chain has a similar trick. Alpha-catenin has a hidden vinculin site of its own, and tension opens it. So both chains can reinforce themselves under load.
scenes.narration: The cadherin chain has a similar trick. α-Catenin has a hidden vinculin site of its own, and tension opens it. So both chains can reinforce themselves under load.
scenes.caption: The cadherin chain has a similar trick. α-Catenin has a hidden vinculin site of its own, and tension opens it. So both chains can reinforce themselves under load.
scenes.visual: Camera pans up the side wall to the adherens chain between two cells from chapter 1: BLUE cadherins meeting in the gap with YELLOW calcium in the joints, TEAL β-catenin and α-catenin blocks, GREEN actin cable. On 'hidden vinculin site', the α-catenin block turns briefly semi-transparent to show a white dot inside. On 'tension opens it', GOLD arrows pull the two cells apart gently; the α-catenin block opens, a TEAL block labelled 'activated vinculin' docks and sends an extra tie to the GREEN cable. Then both chains, integrin below and adherens above, glow at once with their extra vinculin ties (label 'both chains can reinforce').

scenes.tts: But is force the only key? Talin and vinculin each fold shut on their own, hiding their binding sites. This self-closing is called autoinhibition.
scenes.narration: But is force the only key? Talin and vinculin each fold shut on their own, hiding their binding sites. This self-closing is called autoinhibition.
scenes.caption: But is force the only key? Talin and vinculin each fold shut on their own, hiding their binding sites. This self-closing is called autoinhibition.
scenes.visual: Back at the integrin chain. Two labelled TEAL chips, 'talin' and 'vinculin', drift in the cytoplasm. Each starts with a simple open latch icon beside a white binding-site dot; on 'fold shut', the latch closes over the dot. Label 'autoinhibition: sites masked'. A white question 'Is force the only key?' appears at the top. Corner label 'schematic'. Do not draw either protein's molecular shape.

scenes.tts: Researchers tested this in mouse fibroblasts. Normal, autoinhibited talin and vinculin did not bind each other at mitochondria. Releasing either protein's autoinhibition enabled binding without force. Those active forms still supported disorganized adhesions when myosin two was blocked.
scenes.narration: Researchers tested this in mouse fibroblasts. Normal, autoinhibited talin and vinculin did not bind each other at mitochondria. Releasing either protein's autoinhibition enabled binding without force. Those active forms still supported disorganized adhesions when myosin II was blocked.
scenes.caption: Researchers tested this in mouse fibroblasts. Normal, autoinhibited talin and vinculin did not bind each other at mitochondria. Releasing either protein's autoinhibition enabled binding without force. Those active forms still supported disorganized adhesions when myosin II was blocked.
scenes.visual: First show two GREY mitochondria as separate test conditions, labelled 'mitochondrial test: no force'. At left, 'normal forms': a TEAL chip labelled 'wild-type vinculin' is pinned to the outer membrane with its latch closed, while a 'wild-type talin' chip with a closed latch stays away. At right, 'autoinhibition released': opening the latch on either one of the two labelled chips lets the pair dock with a small flash. Use chips and latch icons only, never protein shapes. On 'supported disorganized adhesions', dissolve to a fibroblast on ORANGE fibronectin: CORAL myosin motors grey out and stop, while activated talin-vinculin chips remain in bent, disorganized adhesion streaks. Labels: 'myosin II blocked' and 'adhesions persist, not fully mature'. No GOLD pulse in this scene.

scenes.tts: So force can expose binding sites, while engineered release from autoinhibition can bypass force. Whether a cell's own signals do that at the same steps in a tissue is not known.
scenes.narration: So force can expose binding sites, while engineered release from autoinhibition can bypass force. Whether a cell's own signals do that at the same steps in a tissue is not known.
scenes.caption: So force can expose binding sites, while engineered release from autoinhibition can bypass force. Whether a cell's own signals do that at the same steps in a tissue is not known.
scenes.visual: Two distinct schematic panels appear above the integrin chain. In the left panel, a GOLD arrow labelled 'pull' stretches a talin bundle and exposes a white site. In the right panel, labelled 'engineered fibroblast test', a TEAL latch labelled 'autoinhibition' is released with no GOLD arrow, and talin and vinculin chips dock. Do not imply that the two manipulations open the same structure. On 'not known', a white label 'normal tissue signals: unknown' appears beneath both panels with a small question mark. The CORAL motors resume moving slowly in the background.

scenes.tts: And a few piconewtons on one molecule are not the pull of a whole cell. One more link, where the catenins meet actin, behaves oddly under force. The text picks that up next.
scenes.narration: And a few piconewtons on one molecule are not the pull of a whole cell. One more link, where the catenins meet actin, behaves oddly under force. The text picks that up next.
scenes.caption: And a few piconewtons on one molecule are not the pull of a whole cell. One more link, where the catenins meet actin, behaves oddly under force. The text picks that up next.
scenes.visual: Zoom out from one talin molecule (label 'one molecule: a few pN') to the whole cell spread on the ORANGE matrix with dozens of integrin chains glowing along its base (label 'whole cell: many chains'). Then the camera drifts up to the adherens chain and rests on the joint between TEAL α-catenin and the GREEN actin cable, which flickers with a small white question mark (label 'catenin to actin: next'). Do not show how its bond lifetime changes with force.

scenes.tts: So a chain is more than fixed parts. Some links do not just hold or break; they respond to pull. Pulling can open sites and recruit ties. Engineered release from autoinhibition can bypass force.
scenes.narration: So a chain is more than fixed parts. Some links do not just hold or break; they respond to pull. Pulling can open sites and recruit ties. Engineered release from autoinhibition can bypass force.
scenes.caption: So a chain is more than fixed parts. Some links do not just hold or break; they respond to pull. Pulling can open sites and recruit ties. Engineered release from autoinhibition can bypass force.
scenes.visual: Zoom all the way out to the full world from chapter 1: the row of cells, basement membrane, matrix ropes and gel. All chains glow in their colours; the CORAL motors move, a GOLD pulse spreads through the web, and small TEAL vinculin ties appear along talin and α-catenin as the pulse passes. On 'Engineered release', keep the tissue world unchanged and open a small inset labelled 'engineered test: no force', where releasing a TEAL autoinhibition latch lets talin and vinculin chips dock. The white question 'Can pull change a link?' returns at the top and gains a white answer beneath: 'Sometimes; engineered release bypasses force.'

End card: the take-home line in white over the dimmed world. Beneath it, two small schematic panels share the frame: a GOLD pull exposes a white site in TEAL talin blocks at left; at right, a TEAL autoinhibition latch opens with no GOLD arrow and talin-vinculin chips dock. No molecular structures.
scenes.line: Pull can expose hidden sites; releasing autoinhibition can bypass force.
